title: Thinking Too Much of Thinking
author: TextSavvy
summary: This article challenges what it calls Western education's obsession with 'thinking' as a thing that can be directly taught and developed in students, arguing that the word functions as a placeholder that sounds cognitive and dynamic but obscures the actual mechanism by which better thinking happens. The author points out that every commencement address and education crisis involves someone declaring that schools must 'teach students to think' — but no one ever says schools must 'teach students to digest.' Like digestion, thinking is a natural process influenced by inputs; we cannot tinker with it directly, and pretending we can leads to irresponsible pedagogy. The actual mechanism, the article argues, is knowledge: teach students knowledge, and they will be better thinkers. Thinking is not a generic skill to be exercised in the abstract but a knowledge-dependent process that improves when students have more and better-organized domain knowledge to think with. The article's conclusion is stark: teaching thinking directly is not just futile but outside the legitimate scope of what schools can do — the job has boundaries.
points: The education world's obsession with 'teaching students to think' treats thinking as a standalone skill that can be directly improved — but thinking, like digestion, is a natural process we cannot tinker with directly; we can only influence what students think about.

Knowledge is the actual mechanism: students become better thinkers by learning more and better-organized domain knowledge, not by practicing generic thinking skills or being exposed to thinking frameworks in the abstract.

Treating 'thinking' as a manipulable quantity creates irresponsible pedagogy: it licenses an endless variety of classroom activities that feel cognitively active (discussions, projects, debates) while neglecting the knowledge acquisition that would make those activities substantive.

The commencement-address fallacy: the phrase 'teach students to think' rolls easily off the tongue precisely because no one stops to ask what it means — but a quick parallel ('teach students to digest') reveals the conceptual incoherence immediately.

The job of teaching has genuine limits: a teacher can determine what students think about (by selecting and sequencing knowledge) but cannot directly engineer the quality of the thinking process itself — acknowledging this boundary is a form of professional honesty.
quotes: 'Thinking' seems to be the word one reaches for when they need the process of education to sound really locally dynamic and cognitive—as though something is getting done, now, you know? Some kilojoules of electric brain work are being produced, in the moment and in the abstract, and this something—especially in the abstract—is somehow discernible and directly manipulable by classroom teachers.

Nobel Laureates, captains of industry, cabinet ministers, school superintendents—any one of them is likely to end a commencement address or a discourse on the current crisis by declaring that schools have got to 'teach students to think.' The words roll easily off the tongue and the speakers show not the slightest doubt that the words mean something. But do they?

Why do we never hear about the need to 'teach students to digest'? Like thinking, digestion is a vital natural process, it exhibits large individual differences, and it is influenced by psychological and environmental factors.

No. Teach students knowledge, and they will be better thinkers. We cannot tinker with their thinking directly, and it would not be ethical to do so even if we could. We can influence what they think about. Beyond that, we're just making it up, and that's irresponsible.
The job has boundaries, and that's one of them.

I have been thinking more about 'thinking'—in particular, about what I take to be Western education's obsession with the word. 'Thinking' seems to be the word one reaches for when they need the process of education to sound really locally dynamic and cognitive.
